source_evidence.observation: The source gives the domain and codomain and explicitly requires ψ to be convex and increasing.

source_evidence.anchor: Section 2.7.1, display immediately following the Orlicz-function sentence
source_evidence.observation: The displayed conditions are ψ(0) = 0 and ψ(x) → ∞ as x → ∞.
The examples call ψ(x) = x^p for p ≥ 1 and ψ₂(x) = exp(x²) - 1 Orlicz functions, consistent with the preceding definition on nonnegative arguments.

binders: A function ψ : [0, ∞) → [0, ∞) (PDF page 24; printed page 35, opening sentence of Section 2.7.1).
conclusions: The function ψ is an Orlicz function exactly when it has the listed defining properties: it is convex, it is increasing, ψ(0) = 0, and ψ(x) tends to infinity as x tends to infinity (PDF page 24; printed page 35, definition and following display).
definitions_and_conventions: Both the domain and codomain are the nonnegative half-line [0, ∞), so nonnegativity of values is part of the function type rather than a separately stated condition (PDF page 24; printed page 35, definition's type annotation).
The limit condition is an at-infinity statement along nonnegative real arguments: ψ(x) → ∞ as x → ∞ (PDF page 24; printed page 35, displayed condition).
implicit_context: The definition appears in Section 2.7.1, 'A more general view: Orlicz spaces,' where it is introduced as the datum used to define Orlicz norms and spaces (PDF page 24; printed page 35, section heading and paragraph following the definition).

No probability space, random variable, parameter, or numerical constant is quantified in the Orlicz-function definition itself (PDF page 24; printed page 35, definition before the Orlicz-norm paragraph).

details: ψ maps [0, ∞) to [0, ∞) (PDF page 24; printed page 35, opening definition sentence).
ψ is convex on its nonnegative domain (PDF page 24; printed page 35, opening definition sentence).
ψ is increasing on its nonnegative domain (PDF page 24; printed page 35, opening definition sentence).
ψ vanishes at zero (PDF page 24; printed page 35, displayed condition ψ(0) = 0).
ψ diverges to positive infinity as its argument tends to positive infinity (PDF page 24; printed page 35, displayed limit condition).
This passage is a definition, not an existence theorem or a claim requiring additional hypotheses (PDF page 24; printed page 35, phrase 'is called an Orlicz function if').

undebatable_constraints: The represented function must have nonnegative-real domain and nonnegative-real codomain (PDF page 24; printed page 35, ψ : [0, ∞) → [0, ∞)).
Convexity and increasingness must both be represented on the entire stated domain [0, ∞) (PDF page 24; printed page 35, defining sentence).
The normalization ψ(0) = 0 must be represented (PDF page 24; printed page 35, displayed condition).
The divergence ψ(x) → ∞ as x → ∞ must be represented (PDF page 24; printed page 35, displayed condition).

The Orlicz-function definition itself introduces no random-variable, measure-space, integrability, or finiteness requirement (PDF page 24; printed page 35, definition ending before the Orlicz-norm paragraph).

ambiguities.issue: Whether 'increasing' means nondecreasing or strictly increasing is not made explicit in this passage.
ambiguities.evidence: PDF page 24; printed page 35 uses only the unqualified word 'increasing' in the defining sentence.
ambiguities.impact: A formal target must choose a monotonicity convention. Nondecreasing monotonicity is compatible with the listed examples and the usual convex-analysis usage, while strict monotonicity would be a stronger reading not textually specified here.

ambiguities.issue: The notation [0, ∞) is a subtype-style domain in prose, whereas a formalization may instead use a real-valued function together with restrictions to nonnegative arguments.
ambiguities.evidence: PDF page 24; printed page 35 explicitly types ψ as [0, ∞) → [0, ∞) but states all properties only on that half-line.
ambiguities.impact: Either representation can preserve the source if values and all defining properties on the nonnegative half-line agree; behavior at negative real inputs is outside the source claim.

contract_plain_english: On PDF page 24 (printed page 35), the source defines an Orlicz function to be a function from the nonnegative real half-line to itself that is convex, increasing, zero at zero, and tends to positive infinity as its argument tends to positive infinity. This definition has no random-variable or probability-space assumptions. The word 'increasing' is not explicitly qualified as strict or non-strict.
